passage:
In the office canteen, Dilnaz pushes her lunch box away. 'Six months married, and I haven't had one cup of morning tea in peace,' she tells Vaibhav from accounts. 'Up at five for the family breakfast, home by six for dinner. My mother-in-law says the last bahu gave up her job, so why can't I cut my hours?'
'Do you want to?'
'No. I miss my mother's kitchen, my own routine, everything. But I love this work.'
Her phone buzzes. A message from her husband, Zaid: 'Talked to Ammi. From Monday I cook dinner three nights, so you don't have to rush. And she wants to hear what you think, on Sunday.'
Dilnaz reads it twice and lets out a long breath.

qa.q: By what time does Dilnaz have to be home for dinner?
qa.a: By six.

qa.q: What is Dilnaz feeling as she pushes her lunch box away?
qa.a: She feels worn out and homesick, missing her mother's kitchen and her own routine, and worried about being pushed to cut her work hours.

qa.q: What in Zaid's message could help Dilnaz settle in, and why?
qa.a: He is taking on three dinners and his mother wants to hear Dilnaz's view on Sunday, which shares the work fairly and gives her a voice.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz's mother-in-law see things differently after listening on Sunday?
qa.a: She may realise the job matters deeply to Dilnaz and that what the last bahu did need not be the rule, which could ease the tension.

grounding: Shows a new wife living with her in-laws who has lost her routines, feels pressure over her job and misses her own family, and whose adjustment eases when duties are shared and her voice is invited.

passage:
Dear Ayesha Didi,
It's 11 pm and this is my first quiet minute today. In this house breakfast is at seven sharp, the TV is always on, and I share one wardrobe mirror with three people. I've stopped my evening runs because nobody here goes out after dark, and Mummyji looked surprised when I mentioned my design deadlines. I miss our messy Sunday mornings at home so much.
But one good thing. Last night Rohit said at dinner that we'd take turns with the cooking, and his father agreed. Then Mummyji asked me which days suited me. It's the first time anyone here has asked.
Your little sister,
Ira

qa.q: What time is breakfast in Ira's new home?
qa.a: At seven sharp.

qa.q: What is Ira feeling while writing at 11 pm?
qa.a: Ira feels homesick and a little lost, missing the messy Sunday mornings at home and having given up the evening runs.

qa.q: What changed things for Ira, and why did it help?
qa.a: Rohit suggested taking turns with the cooking and Mummyji asked which days suited Ira; sharing the work and asking her opinion made her feel heard.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ayesha may feel worried about her little sister's loneliness but relieved by the good news at the end, and may want to call soon.

grounding: Illustrates a new wife in her in-laws' home who has given up routines and privacy and misses her own family, and who feels better once duties are shared and her opinion is asked.

Sunday night
Lavanya laughed at me this morning: three video calls before breakfast. Nani's weekly one, Khala asking about her son's college forms, and my cousin Imtiaz showing off his new puppy. I don't mind. Nobody lives in the same lane anymore; we're spread over four cities, so if I don't call, the thread just slips. Last month I took two days' leave when Chhoti Khala was in hospital and slept on the bench beside her bed. Next week is Eid, and the train ticket home is already booked. Living alone here is my choice. Staying close is also my choice, just one I have to keep making.
Rehana

qa.q: How many video calls did Rehana make before breakfast?
qa.a: Three video calls.

qa.q: How does Rehana feel about the effort of keeping in touch?
qa.a: Rehana feels content and committed rather than burdened; the calls are a chosen way to stay close to a family spread over four cities.

qa.q: Which of Rehana's habits keep the family close, and why?
qa.a: Regular calls, turning up in person when Chhoti Khala needed help, and going home for Eid, because closeness now depends on effort, not a shared lane.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see Rehana's morning of calls?
qa.a: Lavanya may find it funny or tiring at first, but might also admire how much Rehana cares for relatives who live far away.

grounding: Shows a young adult living separately who keeps close ties with the extended family through calls, festivals and practical support, treating closeness as a choice kept by effort.

'Say buenos días to Don Rafael,' Mamá whispers on the stairs of their building in Guadalajara. Alejandro, five, shouts, 'Buenos días, Don Rafael!' as proudly as he says 'dinosaur'. The old man tips his hat and chuckles. Upstairs, Alejandro practises on his teddy: 'Don Teddy. Doña Teddy.'
That evening Mamá's friend Lupe visits, and he greets her with 'Don Lupe!' Everyone giggles.
'Tía Lupe,' Mamá corrects gently. 'Tía is for people we love like family.'
Alejandro thinks about it, then climbs into Lupe's lap. 'Tía Lupe,' he tries again, softer this time.

qa.q: What did Alejandro call Lupe at first?
qa.a: 'Don Lupe!'

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling when he said 'Tía Lupe' softly and climbed into her lap?
qa.a: He felt warm and affectionate, starting to sense that 'tía' means someone loved like family, not just a fun sound.

qa.q: What did Mamá's correction get right?
qa.a: She corrected gently, without shaming him, and explained what 'tía' means, so Alejandro could link the word to warmth.

qa.q: How might Don Rafael feel when Alejandro greets him so loudly on the stairs?
qa.a: Don Rafael seems amused and pleased; being greeted with a respectful title by a small child makes him feel noticed.

grounding: Illustrates a young child who is taught respectful titles for older people, copies the sounds first, and only later begins to feel the warmth they carry.

passage: You think answering back is brave, Mahima? Listen to your Nani Madhuri. I was ten. My cousin broke Chachaji's clock, and Chachaji dragged me into the courtyard and scolded me in front of everyone. I knew I hadn't done it. My mouth opened and shut. In our house, answering an elder was worse than breaking ten clocks. So I stood there, eyes on my feet, and said nothing. For years after, I touched his feet at every festival, and every time something small and hot sat in my chest. When he was old he said once, 'You were always the quiet one.' I wish I had told him the truth that day, politely.

qa.q: What did the cousin break?
qa.a: Chachaji's clock.

qa.q: What did young Madhuri feel while standing silent in the courtyard?
qa.a: She felt afraid and ashamed, and also wronged, because she knew she hadn't done it but believed answering an elder was worse.

qa.q: At what moment in the story could a different choice have helped young Madhuri, and what might it have been?
qa.a: Later that same day, she could have told Chachaji calmly and politely that she had not broken the clock, or asked another adult to help her say it.

qa.q: How might Chachaji have seen young Madhuri's silence?
qa.a: Chachaji probably took it as respect or guilt, never knowing she was hurting, which is why years later he only called her 'the quiet one'.

grounding: Illustrates a child who stays silent under an unfair scolding because answering back is seen as disrespect, and whose swallowed hurt later turns into resentment.

Class 5 note, Thursday. Imran, class teacher.
During our lesson on families, Bidisha put her hand up and asked, 'Why do grown-ups say "Respect your elders" every time they're losing an argument?' A few children laughed. She went red but didn't take the question back. After class she told me her Ma says it whenever she asks why she can't go to the park with friends. I explained that respect means being polite and caring, like not shouting and helping an elder carry things, not being scared or never asking questions. She asked if she could still say 'I don't agree' nicely. I said yes, and we practised it once. I will mention our talk to her Ma at the parent meeting.

qa.q: What did Bidisha practise with Imran?

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when a few children laughed at her question?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, going red, but also determined, since she didn't take the question back.

qa.q: What did Imran's explanation give Bidisha?
qa.a: A clear meaning of respect as courtesy and care rather than fear, plus a polite way to disagree, so she can keep her manners and her voice.

qa.q: How might Bidisha's Ma see things after hearing about this at the parent meeting?
qa.a: Her Ma might realise that 'respect your elders' leaves Bidisha feeling shut down, and try giving real reasons about the park instead.

grounding: Illustrates a child who is told to respect elders whenever adults disagree, and a teacher who explains respect as courtesy and care rather than fear.

passage:
In Class 10 geography, Sharma Sir wrote that the Tropic of Cancer passes through Kerala. Disha's hand shot up. 'Sir, that's wrong! It goes through Madhya Pradesh. It's in our textbook!'
The class went 'Ooooh.' Sir's ears turned red. 'Sit down. Don't teach me my subject.'
At break Disha fumed to Pema. 'Why can't we correct them when they're wrong? It's just facts.'
Pema shrugged. 'You're right about the map. But you said it like a quiz-show buzzer.'
After the last bell Disha went to the staffroom, textbook open. 'Sir, I think page 42 says otherwise. Could you check?'
Sir looked, sighed, and nodded. The next morning he corrected the board himself.

qa.q: Where did Disha go after the last bell?
qa.a: To the staffroom, with the textbook open.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling at break while talking to Pema?
qa.a: Disha felt frustrated and wronged, sure of the facts and unable to see why a student cannot correct a teacher.

qa.q: What changed when Disha spoke to Sir in the staffroom?
qa.a: Disha spoke privately and politely and asked Sir to check page 42, so he could accept the correction without losing face.

qa.q: How might Sharma Sir have felt when the class went 'Ooooh'?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and challenged in front of everyone, which made him defensive even though the correction was right.

grounding: Shows a teenager honestly asking why a younger person cannot correct an elder who is wrong, and finding that a polite private correction is heard where a public challenge was not.
